extra.message: The ZAP daemon is started with -config api.disablekey=true and -config api.addrs.addr.name=".*" -config api.addrs.addr.regex=true, which disables the API key and allows any IP address to access the ZAP API without authentication.

The ZAP daemon in CI is configured with api.disablekey=true and api.addrs.addr.name='.*' which disables API key authentication and allows any IP address to access the ZAP API. While this is a CI test environment, the ZAP API is completely open.
The JWT HMAC secret key is hardcoded as the string 'secret', which is extremely weak and publicly known as a common default.

The JWT HMAC secret key is hardcoded as 'secret' - an extremely weak, guessable key. This key is used for JWT token creation (line 184) and verification (line 86). An attacker can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, including admin.

The JWT HMAC secret key is hardcoded as 'secret' in the application configuration. This extremely weak key allows attackers to forge valid JWT tokens by signing arbitrary payloads with this known secret.

The User model defines the password column as a plain db.String(80) with no hashing or encryption mechanism. The setup function stores 'admin123' in plaintext (line 63). The login endpoint (line 182) compares passwords in plaintext.

The Customer model stores credit card numbers (ccn) in plaintext in the database. Additionally, seeding code inserts fake CCNs on first startup, and the registration endpoint accepts CCNs from users without encryption.
The Customer model defines the password column as a plain db.String(150) with no hashing or encryption mechanism. Customer passwords are stored in plaintext (encoded but not hashed).

The application creates a default admin user with hardcoded credentials 'admin'/'admin123' on first startup. These credentials are widely known and allow anyone to log in and access all customer data.
The admin user password 'admin123' is stored in plaintext directly in the database during setup. This password is also hardcoded in the source code.
The admin password is stored in plaintext in the database (User model). The User model password column has no hashing applied during initial setup.
Customer passwords are stored as base64-encoded random bytes instead of being hashed. Base64 encoding is reversible (not a hash function), so these passwords are effectively stored in plaintext.
Credit card numbers generated by Faker are stored in plaintext in the database via the Customer model's ccn column without any encryption.

The verify_jwt function uses app.config['SECRET_KEY_HMAC'] which is set to 'secret' — an extremely weak and easily guessable value. All JWT tokens issued by the application are signed with this key, and the same key is used for verification.
The verify_jwt function logs the full decoded JWT token content to stdout via print(). JWT tokens may contain sensitive claims (username, roles, etc.) that should not be logged.

The verify_jwt function prints the decoded JWT token payload to standard output via print(). JWT tokens may contain sensitive user information (username, roles, etc.). In production environments, stdout is typically captured in application logs, leading to exposure of authentication data in log files.

The insecure_verify() function calls jwt.decode(token, verify=False), completely disabling JWT signature verification. This allows any arbitrary JWT token (with any payload and signature) to be accepted as valid.
The insecure_verify function logs the full decoded JWT token to stdout via print().

The 404 error handler (pnf function) takes request.url and embeds it directly into a Jinja2 template string via %s formatting before passing it to render_template_string(). This means if the URL contains Jinja2 template syntax like {{config}} or {{''.__class__.__mro__[2].__subclasses__()}}, it will be evaluated by the template engine, leading to SSTI.

The 404 error handler pnf() constructs a Jinja2 template string by formatting request.url into it via '%s', then passes it to render_template_string(). request.url is user-controlled and can contain Jinja2 template expressions like {{config}} that will be evaluated server-side.

The 404 error handler embeds request.url directly into an HTML string using %s formatting before rendering with render_template_string(). Since the URL is embedded as raw HTML (not in a {{}} expression), any HTML/JavaScript in the URL is rendered without escaping.

The 404 error handler uses %s string formatting to interpolate request.url into a template string, then passes the result to render_template_string(). Since request.url is user-controlled, an attacker can inject Jinja2 template syntax (e.g., {{config}}, {{''.__class__.__mro__[2].__subclasses__()}}) into the URL, which will be evaluated by the template engine. Additionally, Python builtins 'dir', 'help', and 'locals' are passed to the template context, facilitating exploitation.

The 404 error handler injects request.url (user-controlled) into a template via Python % formatting, then passes the result to render_template_string() which processes Jinja2 template syntax. An attacker can include Jinja2 expressions like {{config}} in the request URL to execute arbitrary template code. Additionally, dir, help, and locals are passed as template context variables, providing further attack surface for SSTI exploitation.

The 404 error handler passes Python built-in functions dir, help, and locals to the template context via render_template_string. These can be used in template injection attacks to access application internals and environment variables.
The root '/' endpoint dynamically generates a sitemap listing all registered URL routes, their endpoint names, and allowed HTTP methods. This exposes the complete attack surface of the application.
The /register/user endpoint allows anyone to register a new user account without any authentication or authorization. This creates privileged User accounts (used for login) with no restrictions.
The user registration endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to create unlimited accounts, leading to account enumeration or database resource exhaustion.
The /register/user endpoint allows anyone to register new users without any authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated attacker can create arbitrary user accounts.
The reg_customer() function hashes passwords using MD5, which is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to rainbow table and collision attacks.
The reg_customer() endpoint returns str(e.message) in the JSON error response, exposing internal exception details to the client.
The /register/customer endpoint allows anyone to create customer records including credit card numbers without any authentication.
The customer registration endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to create unlimited customer records.

The /register/customer endpoint allows anyone to register new customer records without authentication. Additionally, users can supply their own credit card number (ccn field) which will be stored in the database.

The /register/customer endpoint stores the password in plaintext to the database. Unlike the /register/user endpoint which uses MD5 hashing (also weak), this endpoint stores the raw password string directly into the Customer model without any hashing.
The reg_user() endpoint returns str(e.message) in the JSON error response, exposing internal exception details.
The /login endpoint has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism. An attacker can brute-force username/password combinations without any restriction.
The login endpoint logs the full request JSON body via print(content). The request body contains the user's password in plaintext, which is written to stdout/logs.

The login endpoint queries the database comparing both username and password as plaintext strings: User.query.filter_by(username=username, password=password). This confirms passwords are stored and compared in plaintext.
The commented-out session cookie on line 186 would have been set without HttpOnly or Secure flags. While this line is commented out, the pattern shows insecure cookie practices.

The fetch_customer() function accepts a customer ID from the request body and returns the customer record without verifying that the authenticated user owns that customer record. Any authenticated user can access any customer's data by specifying any ID.

The fetch_customer endpoint returns the full credit card number (cc_num) in the JSON response to any authenticated user. There is no authorization check to verify the requesting user owns the customer record, and the full PAN is exposed.
The /fetch/customer endpoint returns the customer's credit card number (ccn) in the API response. This exposes sensitive financial data to any authenticated user.

The /get/<cust_id> endpoint relies on the insecure_verify function which always returns True (JWT signature verification disabled). Any request with a non-empty Authorization header (even a completely invalid or forged token) passes authentication, making the authorization check effectively meaningless.

The /get/<cust_id> endpoint uses insecure_verify() which disables JWT signature verification (verify=False) and always returns True. This means any arbitrary token, or even a malformed pseudo-JWT string, will pass authentication. Combined with the fact that no user ownership check is performed on the customer record, this allows complete access to all customer data.

The /get/<cust_id> endpoint uses the insecure_verify function which calls jwt.decode(token, verify=False), completely bypassing JWT signature verification. This means ANY arbitrary JWT token (including self-crafted tokens with forged claims) will be accepted, allowing full authentication bypass.

The get_customer() function retrieves a customer record by ID from the URL path without any ownership verification. Combined with the insecure_verify() function which accepts any token, this endpoint is completely unprotected.
The get_customer endpoint returns the full credit card number (cc_num) in the JSON response. This endpoint uses 'insecure_verify' which bypasses JWT signature verification entirely (verify=False).
The /get/<cust_id> endpoint returns the customer's credit card number (ccn) in the API response. This exposes sensitive financial data.
The /search endpoint prints the user-supplied search term to stdout. In production this could leak sensitive search patterns.

User-controlled search input is directly concatenated into a SQL query string using string formatting. The 'search' field from the JSON request body is inserted into the SQL query via % string formatting, enabling SQL injection.

The /search endpoint's error handler injects the error message string into a template via %s formatting and passes it to render_template_string(). Error messages can contain user-controlled data reflecting search terms, enabling cross-site scripting attacks. Additionally, Jinja2 expressions in errors would be evaluated (SSTI).

The search_customer() error handler takes str(e) (the exception message, which contains the user's search term from SQL injection attempt) and embeds it directly into a Jinja2 template string via %s formatting before passing it to render_template_string(). Any Jinja2 syntax in the exception message will be evaluated.
When a SQL error occurs in the search endpoint, the full database error message (including the executed SQL query) is rendered in the HTML response to the user.

The search_customer() error handler constructs a Jinja2 template string by formatting the exception message str(e) via '%s', then passes it to render_template_string(). The exception message can contain user-controlled input from the search term, which when crafted can include Jinja2 template expressions.

The search error handler embeds the exception message str(e) directly into an HTML string using %s formatting. The exception message contains the user's search term, meaning attacker-controlled HTML/JS is rendered without escaping.

When the /search endpoint throws an exception (e.g., during SQL injection), the error message string is injected into a template via % formatting and passed to render_template_string(), which processes Jinja2 template syntax. If an attacker can control the error message content (which is possible through SQL injection), they can achieve SSTI. Additionally, dir, help, and locals are passed as template context variables.
The search_customer error handler passes Python built-in functions dir, help, and locals to the template context via render_template_string.

The /xxe_uploader endpoint accepts POST requests with file uploads and processes them with python-docx, but there is no authentication check at all. Any unauthenticated attacker can upload files to be processed.
The /xxe_uploader endpoint processes file uploads with no authentication or authorization check. Anyone can upload files to the server.

The /xxe_uploader endpoint uses random.randint(1, 100) to generate a random prefix for uploaded filenames. This uses Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG (not cryptographically secure) with only 100 possible values, making the output easily predictable. An attacker can enumerate or predict uploaded file locations.

The /xxe_uploader endpoint accepts file uploads and processes them with the python-docx library's Document() function. The python-docx library parses XML within DOCX files, and the installed version of lxml (4.2.1) may not have safe XML parsing defaults, making it vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) attacks.

The /yaml_hammer endpoint accepts YAML file uploads (POST) with no authentication check whatsoever. This endpoint saves uploaded files and then deserializes them with unsafe yaml.load(), which can execute arbitrary code.
The /yaml_hammer endpoint processes YAML file uploads with no authentication or authorization check.

The /yaml_hammer endpoint uses random.randint(1, 100) to generate a random prefix for uploaded YAML filenames. Same weak PRNG issue as /xxe_uploader - only 100 possible values using Python's predictable Mersenne Twister.

The yaml_hammer endpoint uses yaml.load(y) to deserialize user-uploaded YAML file contents without any restrictions. PyYAML's yaml.load() is unsafe and can deserialize arbitrary Python objects, leading to Remote Code Execution.
